item.title: Can Your Environment Cause Schizophrenia?
item.description:
Psychosis

Can Your Environment Cause Schizophrenia?

A dive into epigenetics and the development of schizophrenia.

Posted June 5, 2026

Key points
  • Schizophrenia is a neurodevelopmental disorder.
  • Epigenetic processes, which feature gene-environment interactions, cause brain-alterations.
  • Treatment should include early intervention, CBTp, behavioral strategies, and environmental stabilization.

By Jadin Marshall, MS, and Erica D. Marshall-Lee, Ph.D., ABPP, on behalf of the Atlanta Behavioral Health Advocates.

Source: Nothing Ahead/Pexels

Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness that is characterized by disruptions in one’s thought processes, emotional range, behaviors, sensory-perceptual experiences, and adaptive functioning (Tandon et al., 2009; Patel et al., 2014).

When diagnosing schizophrenia, there is often an observable pattern around trauma and stress histories. Oftentimes, individuals with schizophrenia have histories that include chronic stress, family conflict, constant upheaval, abuse, neglect, etc. (Read et al., 2005). Often these stressful experiences occur during late adolescent and early adulthood (Patel et al., 2014). The question then becomes: how do these experiences lead to lasting changes in the brain? Some evidence suggests that Schizophrenia is considered to be a neurodevelopmental disorder (Rapoport et al., 2005; Stachowiak et al., 2013; Schmitt et al., 2023). This means there is abnormal brain development during gestation or early life. Epigenetics can play a crucial role in this development.

Epigenetics is the study of how the environment and behaviors can alter gene expression without altering the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence.

Here’s a breakdown of how it works, with an epigenetic process called DNA methylation:

Inside every cell, DNA is tightly wrapped around proteins called histones. When DNA wraps around the proteins, it results in a larger structure called chromatin. When the DNA and proteins are tightly packed, the DNA is not as accessible and therefore cannot be read, meaning the region is “turned off” (Moore et al., 2013).

Importantly, these processes are responsive to the environment. So, experiences, such as chronic stress or trauma, can lead to these chemical modifications and, in turn, shape how certain genes are expressed.

The diathesis-stress model adds to the explanation of these changes. The diathesis-stress model is a framework that proposes that someone with a biological vulnerability to schizophrenia who experiences enough stress or environmental adversity can trigger a disorder (Walker & Diforio, 1997; Pruessner et al., 2017). While the diathesis-stress model explains how adversity precipitates psychosis in biologically vulnerable individuals, epigenetics helps explain how the biological process of stress becomes embedded within the body.

A system implicated in these processes is the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. The HPA axis is the main stress response system and connects how the brain perceives and the body responds to stress. Short-term activation can be adaptive, but chronic activation can lead to dysregulation in the brain due to excessive stress (Dunlavey, 2018).

HPA-axis dysregulation is relevant to psychosis and the development of schizophrenia because prolonged stress, by dysregulating the brain, can increase sensitivity to future stressors. This process, in turn, increases perceptions of threat and may lead individuals to assign particular significance to irrelevant or unimportant stimuli (Pruessner et al., 2017). According to Mikulska et al. (2021), “increased susceptibility to environmental stress in childhood has been shown to lead to hyperreactivity of the HPA axis in response to acute stress [...] therefore, [contributing] to the development of psychosis.” (p. 12). Walker et al. (2008) supports this claim as well.

Consider driving a car as an analogy for this process: In this case, the diathesis stress model is synonymous with driving a car that breaks down. An individual's biological vulnerability serves as a car that is, from the start, more difficult to steer. Potholes, random objects, and uneven lanes act as chronic stress. The car's suspension acts as an epigenetic mechanism, such as DNA methylation. If the driver struggles with the steering due to its sensitivity, continues to run over potholes, and the suspension begins to fail, the car will be susceptible to a breakdown.

Here’s a clinical example:

Grey, a 25-year-old female, resides in a home with her mother and grandmother. Her grandmother was diagnosed with schizophrenia, her mother has an alcohol abuse disorder, and her father’s diagnosis is unknown due to his absence in Grey’s life. Overall, she had an unpredictable home environment. Her body learned early that it needed to stay alert. Over time, however, the repeated stress due to her environment led to epigenetic changes in her stress response system (HPA Axis). That means, biologically, her stress system had a hard time turning off, and her brain stayed in a state of heightened arousal. Over time, the brain started assigning importance to things that were neutral. She heard a random noise; that must have meant something. Symptoms started to emerge due to the overactivation of her stress system, genetic vulnerability, and possible internal epigenetic change. Paranoia, delusions, and even perceptual disturbances began to affect Grey.

What does that change about how schizophrenia is understood? Maybe the difference between who develops schizophrenia and who doesn’t isn’t as fixed as we’d like to believe.

Here are some tangible ways to take initiative:

For those struggling with first-episode psychosis, regulate stress daily. This can look like taking part in deep breathing exercises at home or even a fun yoga class! Protect your sleep. Sleep disruptions can increase stress hormones. So, be consistent with sleep-wake time, get a full eight hours, limit caffeine six hours prior to bed, and no bedtime scrolling on TikTok! Be mindful of substance usage. Cannabis can interact negatively with your dopamine system, increasing the risk of psychosis, especially as it develops (Ahrens et al., 2025). Try a more adaptive coping skill, like journaling, or a hands-on activity like pottery or other crafts. Lastly, try to create a stable environment. Supportive friends and family are helpful in reducing extra stress.

We can’t change DNA or eliminate all the stress we experience, but we can change how we respond to stress.

If biology can be shaped by experience, then treatment isn’t just about managing symptoms. It’s about changing the conditions that shape biology in the first place.
